Navin's rules for this task (follow every one):
[G-01] Everything taught comes from the book. Knowledge from outside the book is allowed only to explain the book better; it is marked as outside, standard textbook-level and correct. Never invent facts, numbers, names or quotations.
[G-02] Work like the best teacher of these learners and this exam, not like a summariser. Depth beats brevity: nothing teachable on the page is skipped or compressed away, and every explanation makes a student understand, not just remember.
[G-03] Before the output, fill 'notes' with brief notes for the reviewer and for Navin: what this unit is about, the key questions a teacher must answer about it, the main decisions you made with a one-line reason each, and anything uncertain. Keep the notes short; they explain the work, they are not the work.
[G-05] Never shorten work to fit a length. If a unit of work is too large, it is split by BIE into smaller units; within a unit, completeness wins.
[S1-01] Read the page with two eyes: the native text blocks (exact words and numbers) and the page image (tables, diagrams, labels, arrows, equations, layout). Items that exist only in the image are as important as text items. A page whose text layer is empty or nearly empty is read entirely from the image.
[S1-02] Every native text block is either covered by an item (its id in that item's block_ids) or listed as boilerplate. Boilerplate is only running headers, page numbers, publisher adverts, contact lines and watermarks; nothing teachable is boilerplate.
[S1-03] Every table becomes one 'table' item plus one 'table_row' item per row, in order, each row's content giving every cell with its column header, for example 'Smooth muscle | Location: G.I. tract, uterus, eye, blood vessels | Function: peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size, erects hairs | Appearance: no striations, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary'. [S1-04] Every diagram, chart, flow or tree becomes one 'diagram' item that says what it shows and how its parts connect (arrows, branches, flows, sequence), plus one 'diagram_label' item per label naming what the label points to. A classification tree lists every branch and leaf with its parent.
[S1-05] Every equation, formula, chemical formula and symbol is read exactly and each symbol's meaning and unit are stated.
[S1-06] Understand every teachable item by questioning it like a teacher. Ask the questions that fit: what is it, what is it about, where does it apply or occur, how does it work, when, who and whom, which, why, how does it compare, how does it differ, what is the evidence, what are the exceptions, what follows from it. Then keep asking 'why' and 'how' on your own answers (depth 2, 3 ...) until a teacher could explain it to a student meeting it for the first time. Answers explain; they never just repeat the item's words.
[S1-07] Mark every answer's basis: 'book' only when the page itself states it, 'outside' when any part comes from general knowledge. Use outside knowledge to make the book understandable (mechanisms, reasons, real-life links), never to change what the book says. [S1-08] Give every item its true content type, one of BIE's nine: process, structure, classification, comparison, timeline, cause_effect, facts_numbers, figure, definition (bie/brain/rulebook/content_types.json). [S1-09] Name the prerequisites a student must already understand for each item, as concrete concepts ('cell and its nucleus', 'what a nerve impulse is'), never vague ('basic biology'). Prerequisites are taught later, not just listed.
[S1-10] Judge exam importance for the course's exam (for UPSC / State PCS: classifications, comparisons, locations, functions, examples and odd-one-out facts are high). Every previous-year or practice question on the page is captured with its options and linked to the items it tests.

BIE's content types (the type of an item decides its required questions and how it is taught, shown, played and drawn):
- process · Process: Something that happens in steps or stages over time: a mechanism, a procedure, a cycle (photosynthesis, cell division, how a bill becomes law). Required questions: how (kaise), when (kab). Other questions: what (kya), where (kahan), why (kyun), consequence (nateeja).
- structure · Structure: Something made of parts arranged in space, each part with a function (a cell, a leaf, the heart, a machine, the Parliament). Required questions: what (kya), where (kahan). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun), which (kaun).
- classification · Classification: A group divided into kinds by a stated basis (types of tissues, kinds of rocks, kinds of writs). Required questions: which (kaun), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot), where (kahan).
- comparison · Comparison: Two or more things set side by side on stated criteria (plant and animal cells, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Required questions: compare (tulna), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), why (kyun), evidence (saboot).
- timeline · Timeline: Events placed in time: history, the development of an idea, stages of a life (the Revolt of 1857, evolution of cell theory). Required questions: when (kab), why (kyun). Other questions: who (kaun), where (kahan), consequence (nateeja).
- cause_effect · Reasoning (cause and effect): Why something happens: causes, effects, conditions and chains of reasoning (why tissues specialise, why prices rise, why a law was needed). Required questions: why (kyun), how (kaise). Other questions: consequence (nateeja), evidence (saboot), exception (tulna).
- facts_numbers · Facts and numbers: Stated facts, quantities, measurements, statistics and formulas (heart rate 72 per minute, 3,000 against 50,000 soldiers at Plassey, F = ma). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: compare (tulna), why (kyun).
- figure · Figure: A diagram, photo, map, graph or table drawing on the page whose content is visual (tissue pages 2, 7 and 8 are figures only). Required questions: what (kya), which (kaun). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun).
- definition · Definition: A term and its meaning as the book states it (tissue, meristem, sovereignty). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: about (kya), why (kyun).

output.page_summary: Tissues are groups of cells performing a shared function and enable division of labour within a hierarchy from cells to organisms. The page compares mitosis with meiosis, contrasts plant and animal mitosis, and divides plant tissues into meristematic and permanent tissues, with their visible subtypes and components.

items.content: 10. Tissues and Its Types
items.exam_note: Chapter heading.

items.content: TISSUE: Cells combine to perform same function.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the page mean by tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: A tissue is a grouping of cells that work together to perform the same function.

teacher_understanding.question: What defining feature does the page give for recognising a tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: It links the combination of cells to their shared function; merely naming a collection of cells leaves out this functional connection.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a group of cells function as a tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cells coordinate their activities and contribute to a common task. For example, muscle cells collectively produce contraction.

prerequisites: cell as a unit of life
items.exam_note: Foundational definition for distinguishing cells, tissues and organs.

items.content: • When plant cells combine, they form plant tissues.

teacher_understanding.question: Which cells form plant tissues?
teacher_understanding.answer: Plant tissues are formed by the combination of plant cells.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this category differ from animal tissue on the page?
teacher_understanding.answer: The distinction here is the kind of organism supplying the cells: plant cells form plant tissues, while animal cells form animal tissues.

teacher_understanding.question: How should 'combine' be understood in a growing plant?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cells produced during growth remain organised into groups and may differentiate for common functions; the wording need not imply that separate cells fuse into one cell.

items.exam_note: Introduces the plant-tissue classification.

items.content: • When animal cells combine, they form animal tissues.

teacher_understanding.question: Which cells form animal tissues?
teacher_understanding.answer: Animal tissues are formed from animal cells acting together.

teacher_understanding.question: What separates animal tissues from plant tissues in these introductory bullets?
teacher_understanding.answer: Animal tissues consist of animal cells; plant tissues consist of plant cells.

teacher_understanding.question: How can animal cells contribute to a common tissue function?
teacher_understanding.answer: They acquire specialised properties and coordinate their activity, as nerve cells do in receiving and transmitting signals.

items.exam_note: Basic distinction between plant and animal tissues.

items.content: • Causes division of labour.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does the page connect tissues with division of labour?
teacher_understanding.answer: It presents tissue formation as enabling cells to share the work of the organism.

teacher_understanding.question: How does division of labour operate between tissues?
teacher_understanding.answer: Different tissues specialise in different tasks, such as protection, transport or movement, so the organism's work is distributed among specialised groups.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can specialisation improve performance?
teacher_understanding.answer: A cell's shape, internal machinery and activity can be suited to a particular task, improving its contribution to that task while other cells perform complementary roles.

items.exam_note: Explains the functional significance of tissues.

items.content: • Decreases workload on individual cells, hence leads to organisation.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does the page say tissues decrease the workload on individual cells?
teacher_understanding.answer: It connects grouping cells into tissues with distributing work, rather than placing the organism's work on individual cells.

teacher_understanding.question: How does distributing work lead to organisation?
teacher_understanding.answer: Specialised cells form tissues; different tissues cooperate in organs; organs cooperate in organ systems. This produces coordinated levels of organisation.

teacher_understanding.question: Does reduced workload mean a specialised cell stops carrying out its own life processes?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. It still maintains itself, including using energy and synthesising required molecules. The shared workload concerns the wider functions of the organism.

items.exam_note: Conceptual explanation of multicellular organisation.

items.content: Cell → Tissues → Organ → Organ system → Organisms. Each rightward arrow connects a smaller biological level to the larger level into which it is organised.

teacher_understanding.question: What hierarchy does the sequence show?
teacher_understanding.answer: It orders biological organisation from cell to tissue, organ, organ system and organism.

teacher_understanding.question: Where are tissues and organs placed in the hierarchy?
teacher_understanding.answer: Tissues lie between cells and organs; organs lie between tissues and organ systems.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the arrows be interpreted?
teacher_understanding.answer: They express organisational membership: cells make up tissues, tissues make up organs, and organs work in systems within an organism. They do not mean that one isolated cell simply turns into an entire organism through these named stages.

items.exam_note: Important ordering and relationship question.

items.content: Cell: first level; arrow leads to Tissues.

teacher_understanding.question: What does Cell name here?
teacher_understanding.answer: The starting level in the organisation sequence.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is Cell positioned?
teacher_understanding.answer: Before Tissues, at the left end.

teacher_understanding.question: How do cells contribute to the next level?
teacher_understanding.answer: Groups of cells coordinate a shared function to form a tissue.

items.exam_note: Starting level of the printed hierarchy.

items.content: Tissues: between Cell and Organ.

teacher_understanding.question: What does Tissues identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: The level formed by cells and preceding organs.

teacher_understanding.question: Where are tissues in the sequence?
teacher_understanding.answer: After Cell and before Organ.

teacher_understanding.question: How can tissues contribute to an organ?
teacher_understanding.answer: Different tissues cooperate in an organ; for example, muscle, connective and nervous tissues contribute to the heart.

items.exam_note: Distinguish tissue from organ.

items.content: Organ: between Tissues and Organ system.

teacher_understanding.question: What does Organ represent?
teacher_understanding.answer: The organisational level between tissues and organ systems.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is Organ placed?
teacher_understanding.answer: After Tissues and before Organ system.

teacher_understanding.question: How is an organ organised internally?
teacher_understanding.answer: Several tissues are arranged to perform related functions, as in a leaf or a heart.

items.exam_note: Common distinction in levels of organisation.

items.content: Organ system: between Organ and Organisms.

teacher_understanding.question: What does Organ system identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: The level above an organ and below the complete organism.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is Organ system in the sequence?
teacher_understanding.answer: Between Organ and Organisms.

teacher_understanding.question: How do organs function together as a system?
teacher_understanding.answer: They perform complementary tasks within a larger function; digestive organs, for example, cooperate in processing food and absorbing nutrients.

items.exam_note: Useful for ordering and examples.

items.content: Organisms: final level, following Organ system.

teacher_understanding.question: What does Organisms name at the end?
teacher_understanding.answer: The complete living beings at the highest level shown.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is this label located?
teacher_understanding.answer: At the right end, after Organ system.

teacher_understanding.question: How do systems support an organism?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their activities are coordinated so that needs such as nutrition, transport and waste removal are met together.

items.exam_note: Endpoint of the hierarchy shown; the sequence concerns multicellular organisation.

items.content: Two-column comparison headed Mitosis and Meiosis, containing 11 numbered comparison rows.
items.exam_note: Major comparison table; row 9 requires explicit correction during teaching.

items.content: 1) Mitosis: It occurs in somatic cells. | Meiosis: It occurs in germ cells.

teacher_understanding.question: Which cell categories does the table associate with the two divisions?
teacher_understanding.answer: It associates mitosis with somatic cells and meiosis with germ cells.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the distinction between somatic and germ cells?
teacher_understanding.answer: Somatic cells are body cells outside the reproductive germ line; germ-line cells give rise to reproductive cells.

teacher_understanding.question: Why must this row be treated as a simplified association?
teacher_understanding.answer: Germ-line cells can also multiply by mitosis. In plants, meiosis produces spores in spore mother cells, so the row is not a complete description of every life cycle.

items.exam_note: Frequently tested association; avoid treating it as an exclusive rule.

items.content: 2) Mitosis: Nucleus divides only once. | Meiosis: Nucleus divides twice.

teacher_understanding.question: How many nuclear divisions occur in each?
teacher_understanding.answer: Mitosis has one nuclear division; meiosis has two.

teacher_understanding.question: What are the two meiotic divisions called?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are meiosis I and meiosis II.

teacher_understanding.question: How do the two meiotic divisions accomplish different separations?
teacher_understanding.answer: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes, whereas meiosis II separates sister chromatids.

items.exam_note: Core numerical and mechanistic distinction.

items.content: 3) Mitosis: Two daughter cells are formed. | Meiosis: Four daughter cells are formed.

teacher_understanding.question: What daughter-cell counts are printed?
teacher_understanding.answer: The table gives two for mitosis and four for meiosis.

teacher_understanding.question: How do these outcomes differ?
teacher_understanding.answer: The typical meiotic outcome has twice as many products as a single mitotic division.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the division pattern account for the counts?
teacher_understanding.answer: One division usually gives two products; in meiosis, both products of the first division undergo a second division, giving four. Unequal cytokinesis in animal egg formation means these are not four equivalent functional eggs.

items.exam_note: Standard outcome comparison, with oogenesis qualification.

items.content: 4) Mitosis: Daughter cells are diploid. | Meiosis: Daughter cells are haploid.

teacher_understanding.question: What ploidy does the table assign to the daughter cells?
teacher_understanding.answer: It describes mitotic daughters as diploid and meiotic daughters as haploid.

teacher_understanding.question: How do diploid and haploid differ?
teacher_understanding.answer: Diploid means two chromosome sets, written 2n; haploid means one set, written n. These symbols describe chromosome sets and have no physical unit.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does the mitosis statement require a starting-cell qualification?
teacher_understanding.answer: Mitosis generally preserves the starting ploidy. A diploid parent gives diploid daughters, but a haploid cell can also divide mitotically and produce haploid daughters.

items.exam_note: Test ploidy preservation versus reduction; the printed mitosis claim is conditional.

items.content: 5) Mitosis: It occurs more frequently. | Meiosis: It occurs less frequently.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the table compare frequency?
teacher_understanding.answer: It calls mitosis more frequent and meiosis less frequent.

teacher_understanding.question: Does this row provide a numerical frequency difference?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. It states a qualitative contrast without counts, rates or a specified organism.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is mitosis often more widespread in a growing multicellular organism?
teacher_understanding.answer: Growth and cell replacement require repeated divisions in many tissues, whereas meiosis is restricted to particular reproductive cells and stages. Actual frequencies depend on the organism, tissue and life stage.

items.exam_note: Qualitative generalisation; no numerical rate is supplied.

items.content: 6) Mitosis: Daughter cells form somatic organs. | Meiosis: Daughter cells form gametes.

teacher_understanding.question: What roles does the row assign to the products?
teacher_understanding.answer: Mitotic daughter cells contribute to somatic organs, while meiotic daughter cells are associated with gamete formation.

teacher_understanding.question: How do these roles differ?
teacher_understanding.answer: The row contrasts body formation with reproductive-cell formation.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the gamete statement be qualified for plants?
teacher_understanding.answer: In land plants, meiosis produces haploid spores. These develop into gametophytes that produce gametes through mitosis; meiotic products are therefore not universally gametes.

items.exam_note: Important body-growth versus reproduction distinction, with plant-life-cycle qualification.

items.content: 7) Mitosis: There is only one prophase, one metaphase one anaphase and one telophase. | Meiosis: There are two of each phase and five sub-phases in prophase - 1.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the table compare the division phases?
teacher_understanding.answer: Mitosis has one occurrence of each named phase; meiosis has two, with five sub-phases in prophase I.

teacher_understanding.question: Which phase has the additional subdivision highlighted here?
teacher_understanding.answer: Prophase I of meiosis has five sub-phases.

teacher_understanding.question: How do the phases organise chromosome separation?
teacher_understanding.answer: Chromosomes condense during prophase, align during metaphase, separate during anaphase and reach the poles as division concludes in telophase. Prophase I includes homologous pairing and crossing over; its five standard sub-phases are leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene and diakinesis.

items.exam_note: Phase counts and prophase I subdivisions are useful objective-exam facts.

items.content: 8) Mitosis: Number of chromosomes are not changed in the daughter cells. | Meiosis: Number of chromosomes are reduced to half.

teacher_understanding.question: How do daughter-cell chromosome numbers compare with the starting cell?
teacher_understanding.answer: Mitosis preserves the number, while meiosis reduces it to half.

teacher_understanding.question: Which process is associated with chromosome-number reduction?
teacher_understanding.answer: Meiosis is the reductional process in this comparison.

teacher_understanding.question: How is chromosome number halved in meiosis?
teacher_understanding.answer: Homologous partners separate into different cells in meiosis I, leaving one member of each pair in each product. Meiosis II then separates sister chromatids without a further halving of chromosome sets.

items.exam_note: Central distinction between equational and reduction division.

items.content: 9) Mitosis: Chromosome number doubles at the beginning of each cell division. | Meiosis: Chromosome number is not doubled. It doubles after the end of first meiotic division.

teacher_understanding.question: What timing claims does the printed row make?
teacher_understanding.answer: It claims chromosome number doubles at the beginning of mitotic division and after the first meiotic division. These are the printed claims, not reliable statements of the mechanism.

teacher_understanding.question: What distinction is needed to evaluate this row?
teacher_understanding.answer: Chromosome number and DNA amount differ. DNA replication creates sister chromatids while chromosome number, conventionally counted by centromeres, remains unchanged before their separation.

teacher_understanding.question: How does DNA replication actually relate to mitosis and meiosis?
teacher_understanding.answer: DNA replicates in S phase before mitosis and before meiosis I. There is no intervening S phase of DNA replication between meiosis I and meiosis II. The printed row confuses chromosome number, DNA replication and its timing.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is the claimed doubling after meiosis I especially misleading?
teacher_understanding.answer: Meiosis depends on one replication followed by two divisions. Replicating the genome again between those divisions would not describe the standard meiotic sequence.

items.exam_note: Printed error: teach the distinction between DNA amount and chromosome number, and the absence of replication between meiotic divisions.

items.content: 10) Mitosis: No crossing over in chromosomes. | Meiosis: Crossing over occurs chromosomes.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the table contrast crossing over?
teacher_understanding.answer: It presents crossing over as absent in mitosis and present in meiosis.

teacher_understanding.question: What does crossing over involve in the standard meiotic account?
teacher_understanding.answer: It involves exchange of corresponding DNA segments between non-sister chromatids of paired homologous chromosomes during prophase I.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is crossing over significant?
teacher_understanding.answer: It creates new combinations of alleles on chromosomes and helps establish connections important for homologous chromosome segregation. Rare mitotic recombination means the printed absence should be understood as the usual introductory contrast.

items.exam_note: Crossing over and genetic variation are major examination concepts.

items.content: 11) Mitosis: Equation division. | Meiosis: Reduction division.

teacher_understanding.question: Which division labels are printed?
teacher_understanding.answer: The table prints 'Equation division' for mitosis and 'Reduction division' for meiosis.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the intended distinction between these terms?
teacher_understanding.answer: The standard term for mitosis is equational division: chromosome sets are preserved. Meiosis is reductional overall because chromosome sets are halved.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should the two meiotic divisions be distinguished here?
teacher_understanding.answer: Meiosis I is reductional because homologues separate; meiosis II is equational because sister chromatids separate. Calling meiosis reduction division describes its overall outcome.

items.exam_note: Retain the printed 'Equation' but explain the standard term 'equational'.

items.content: Table 7.3: Difference between mitosis in Plants and Animals. Columns: Plants | Animals. Four comparison rows.
items.exam_note: Contrasts mitotic apparatus, cytokinesis and sites of division.

items.content: Plants: Centrioles are absent. | Animals: Centrioles are present.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the table compare centrioles?
teacher_understanding.answer: It describes centrioles as absent in plants and present in animals.

teacher_understanding.question: Which side of the comparison is associated with centrioles?
teacher_understanding.answer: The animal side.

teacher_understanding.question: How can plant cells divide without the animal-type centriole arrangement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their spindle microtubules can be organised without centriole-containing centrosomes. The printed contrast fits typical higher-plant and animal cells; some plant groups have centrioles or related basal bodies in particular cells.

items.exam_note: Standard plant–animal distinction with taxonomic qualification.

items.content: Plants: Asters are not formed. | Animals: Asters are formed.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the table state about asters?
teacher_understanding.answer: Asters are not formed in plant mitosis but are formed in animal mitosis.

teacher_understanding.question: What is an aster in this comparison?
teacher_understanding.answer: An aster is a star-like array of microtubules radiating from a centrosomal region in a dividing cell.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is the aster difference related to the preceding row?
teacher_understanding.answer: Typical animal centrosomes organise astral microtubules, whereas typical higher-plant cells organise their mitotic spindle without that centrosome-and-aster arrangement.

items.exam_note: Recognise astral versus typical anastral division.

items.content: Plants: Cell division involves formation of a cell plate. | Animals: Cell division involves furrowing and cleavage of cytoplasm.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the table compare cytoplasmic division?
teacher_understanding.answer: Plant cells form a cell plate; animal cells divide by furrowing and cleavage of the cytoplasm.

teacher_understanding.question: How do the directions of these mechanisms differ?
teacher_understanding.answer: A plant cell plate develops centrally and expands outward; an animal cleavage furrow constricts inward from the cell surface.

teacher_understanding.question: Why do plant and animal cells use different mechanisms?
teacher_understanding.answer: The rigid plant cell wall limits pinching, so vesicles build a partition between daughter cells. In animal cells, an actin–myosin contractile ring constricts the cell surface.

teacher_understanding.question: How is this distinct from division of the nucleus?
teacher_understanding.answer: These mechanisms describe cytokinesis, which partitions cytoplasm; mitosis describes the nuclear division that distributes chromosomes.

items.exam_note: High-yield cell-plate versus cleavage-furrow comparison.

items.content: Plants: Occurs mainly at meristem. | Animals: Occurs in tissues throughout the body.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does the table locate mitosis in plants and animals?
teacher_understanding.answer: Mainly at meristems in plants, and in tissues throughout the body in animals.

teacher_understanding.question: What spatial contrast is being made?
teacher_understanding.answer: Plant division is associated mainly with specialised growth regions, while animal division is described as distributed through body tissues.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should 'throughout the body' not be read as every animal cell dividing?
teacher_understanding.answer: Animal tissues differ in their capacity for division; some mature specialised cells have very limited division. Plant cells outside established meristems may also regain division capacity in suitable circumstances.

items.exam_note: Connects sites of mitosis to the meristem classification below.

items.content: Classification of Plant Tissue → Meristematic Tissue and Permanent Tissue. Meristematic Tissue → Apical Meristem, Lateral Meristem, Intercalary Meristem. Permanent Tissue → Simple and Complex. Simple → Paranchyma, Collenchyma, Sclerenchyma. Sclerenchyma → Fibres and Sclereids. Complex → Xylem and Phloem. Visible Xylem components: Tracheids, Vessels (Tracheae), Xylem parenchyma. Visible Phloem components: Sieve tubes, Companion cells, Phloem parenchyma. The bottoms of the component boxes are cropped.

teacher_understanding.question: Which main tissue groups and subgroups does the tree show?
teacher_understanding.answer: Plant tissue divides into meristematic and permanent tissue. Meristematic tissue has apical, lateral and intercalary meristems; permanent tissue divides into simple and complex tissue, with further branches as shown.

teacher_understanding.question: What distinguishes the two main groups and the two permanent-tissue groups?
teacher_understanding.answer: Meristematic cells actively divide; permanent tissues consist of cells differentiated for particular roles and generally no longer actively dividing. Simple tissues mainly contain one cell type, while complex tissues contain several cooperating cell types.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the connecting lines be read?
teacher_understanding.answer: Read downward from a parent to its subtypes or listed components: Fibres and Sclereids belong under Sclerenchyma, while the lower conducting-cell lists belong under Xylem and Phloem respectively.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is it important to distinguish levels in this tree?
teacher_understanding.answer: Apical, lateral and intercalary are meristem types; fibres and sclereids are sclerenchyma forms; sieve tubes and companion cells are phloem components. Treating these labels as equivalent alternatives would lose their parent–child relationships.

items.exam_note: High-yield hierarchy for classification, matching and odd-one-out questions.

items.content: Classification of Plant Tissue: root label; branches to Meristematic Tissue and Permanent Tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: Which groups branch from the root?
teacher_understanding.answer: Meristematic Tissue and Permanent Tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the basis of their distinction?
teacher_understanding.answer: Active division characterises meristematic tissue, while differentiation for particular functions characterises permanent tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the root organise the chart?
teacher_understanding.answer: All lower labels are reached through one of its two principal branches.

items.exam_note: Starting point for the entire classification.

items.content: Meristematic Tissue: child of Classification of Plant Tissue; parent of Apical Meristem, Lateral Meristem and Intercalary Meristem.

teacher_understanding.question: Which meristematic types are shown?
teacher_understanding.answer: Apical, lateral and intercalary meristems.

teacher_understanding.question: How does meristematic tissue differ from permanent tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Meristematic tissue supplies actively dividing cells for growth; permanent tissue is differentiated for particular functions.

teacher_understanding.question: How does meristematic tissue support plant growth?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its cells divide to add new cells, some of which subsequently enlarge and differentiate into permanent tissues.

items.exam_note: Main category and its three positional types.

items.content: Apical Meristem: child of Meristematic Tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: Which main tissue group includes Apical Meristem?
teacher_understanding.answer: Meristematic Tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How does apical meristem differ in location and growth role from lateral meristem?
teacher_understanding.answer: Apical meristems occur at root and shoot tips and support primary growth in length; lateral meristems occur along the sides and support growth in girth.

teacher_understanding.question: How does an apical meristem lengthen a root or shoot?
teacher_understanding.answer: It produces new cells near the tip; subsequent cell elongation and differentiation contribute to extension.

items.exam_note: Match meristem with tip location and increase in length.

items.where_on_page: chart, yellow box beneath Meristematic Tissue
items.content: Lateral Meristem: child of Meristematic Tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: Which branch contains Lateral Meristem?
teacher_understanding.answer: The Meristematic Tissue branch.

teacher_understanding.question: How does lateral meristem differ from apical meristem?
teacher_understanding.answer: Lateral meristems extend along the sides of stems or roots and contribute to thickness; apical meristems lie at tips and contribute to length.

teacher_understanding.question: How can lateral meristems increase girth?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cambial tissues produce new cells toward the inside or outside, adding tissue layers around the organ.

items.exam_note: Match lateral meristem with secondary growth and girth.

items.content: Intercalary Meristem: child of Meristematic Tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: Which category contains Intercalary Meristem?
teacher_understanding.answer: Meristematic Tissue, alongside apical and lateral meristems.

teacher_understanding.question: How does intercalary meristem differ in position from apical meristem?
teacher_understanding.answer: Intercalary meristems occur between more mature tissues, commonly near leaf bases or internode bases in grasses; apical meristems occur at growing tips.

teacher_understanding.question: How can intercalary meristems help grasses regrow after cutting?
teacher_understanding.answer: Dividing cells at retained basal growth regions can continue producing new tissue even when upper portions have been removed.

items.exam_note: Location and grass-regrowth association are useful matching facts.

items.content: Permanent Tissue: child of Classification of Plant Tissue; parent of Simple and Complex.

teacher_understanding.question: Which two groups branch from Permanent Tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Simple and Complex.

teacher_understanding.question: How is permanent tissue distinguished from meristematic tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Permanent-tissue cells have differentiated for particular roles and generally ceased active division; meristematic cells retain active division.

teacher_understanding.question: How does permanent tissue arise?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cells produced by meristems enlarge and differentiate, acquiring structures suited to roles such as support, storage or transport.

items.exam_note: Principal tissue category and parent of simple and complex tissues.

items.content: Simple: child of Permanent Tissue; parent of Paranchyma, Collenchyma and Sclerenchyma.

teacher_understanding.question: Which simple permanent tissues are listed?
teacher_understanding.answer: Paranchyma, Collenchyma and Sclerenchyma, using the chart's spellings.

teacher_understanding.question: How does simple tissue differ from complex tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Simple tissue consists mainly of one cell type, while complex tissue combines several cell types in a shared function.

teacher_understanding.question: Why are all three labels grouped under Simple?
teacher_understanding.answer: Each is recognised as a tissue primarily characterised by one general type of cell, despite variations within that type.

items.exam_note: Memorise the simple-tissue membership and classification criterion.

items.content: Complex: child of Permanent Tissue; parent of Xylem and Phloem.

teacher_understanding.question: Which complex tissues are shown?
teacher_understanding.answer: Xylem and Phloem.

teacher_understanding.question: What distinguishes complex from simple permanent tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Complex tissue contains different cell types working together, whereas simple tissue is mainly composed of one cell type.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the chart illustrate this complexity?
teacher_understanding.answer: It lists several named components beneath each of Xylem and Phloem, showing that each includes multiple components.

items.exam_note: Xylem and phloem are complex permanent tissues.

items.content: Paranchyma: child of Simple under Permanent Tissue; spelling as printed.

teacher_understanding.question: Which category contains the label Paranchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: Simple permanent tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the tissue intended by this label differ from sclerenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: The standard term is parenchyma. Its cells are generally living and have relatively thin primary walls; sclerenchyma commonly has thick lignified walls and cells dead at maturity.

teacher_understanding.question: How can parenchyma serve different functions?
teacher_understanding.answer: Living cells can store materials, and chloroplast-containing forms can photosynthesise. Their functions depend on location and specialisation.

items.exam_note: Recognise the printed spelling as referring to parenchyma.

items.content: Collenchyma: child of Simple under Permanent Tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is Collenchyma classified?
teacher_understanding.answer: Under Simple permanent tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How does collenchyma differ from parenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: Collenchyma has living cells with unevenly thickened primary walls suited to support, whereas typical parenchyma has relatively thin primary walls.

teacher_understanding.question: How does collenchyma support growing parts?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its thickened but flexible walls provide strength while allowing bending and continued growth in young organs.

items.exam_note: Simple-tissue membership and flexible-support role.

items.content: Sclerenchyma: child of Simple under Permanent Tissue; parent of Fibres and Sclereids.

teacher_understanding.question: Which two forms branch from Sclerenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: Fibres and Sclereids.

teacher_understanding.question: How does sclerenchyma differ from collenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: Sclerenchyma typically has thick lignified secondary walls and cells dead at maturity; collenchyma has living cells with unevenly thickened primary walls.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is sclerenchyma suited to mechanical strength?
teacher_understanding.answer: Thick lignified walls resist deformation and reinforce mature plant parts.

items.exam_note: Links simple tissue to its fibre and sclereid forms.

items.where_on_page: chart, yellow box below-left of Sclerenchyma
items.content: Fibres: child of Sclerenchyma.

teacher_understanding.question: Which tissue is the parent of Fibres here?
teacher_understanding.answer: Sclerenchyma.

teacher_understanding.question: How do fibres generally differ from sclereids?
teacher_understanding.answer: Fibres are usually long, narrow cells with tapering ends; sclereids are commonly shorter and more varied in shape.

teacher_understanding.question: How do fibres strengthen plant parts?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their elongated, thick-walled cells often occur in groups and help resist pulling and bending forces.

items.exam_note: Distinguish fibres from sclereids within sclerenchyma.

items.where_on_page: chart, yellow box below-right of Sclerenchyma
items.content: Sclereids: child of Sclerenchyma.

teacher_understanding.question: Which parent tissue contains Sclereids?
teacher_understanding.answer: Sclerenchyma, alongside Fibres.

teacher_understanding.question: How are sclereids distinguished from fibres?
teacher_understanding.answer: Sclereids tend to be shorter or irregularly shaped, whereas fibres are characteristically elongated.

teacher_understanding.question: How do sclereids contribute to hardness?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their thick lignified walls give local rigidity; stone cells in pear flesh provide a familiar example of their gritty texture.

items.exam_note: Useful subtype, shape and example association.

items.content: Xylem: child of Complex under Permanent Tissue. Visible listed components: Tracheids; Vessels (Tracheae); Xylem parenchyma. Lower box edge is cropped.

teacher_understanding.question: Which visible components are listed under Xylem?
teacher_understanding.answer: Tracheids, Vessels (Tracheae) and Xylem parenchyma.

teacher_understanding.question: How does xylem differ functionally from phloem?
teacher_understanding.answer: Xylem chiefly transports water and mineral nutrients; phloem transports organic assimilates such as sugars between sources and sinks.

teacher_understanding.question: How can one complex tissue combine transport with other roles?
teacher_understanding.answer: Different component cells specialise in conduction, storage or support. The visible crop should not be treated as an exhaustive list of xylem cell types.

items.exam_note: High-yield complex-tissue membership and transport role; list is cropped.

items.where_on_page: chart, Xylem box, first visible component
items.content: Tracheids: listed component of Xylem.

teacher_understanding.question: Which tissue contains Tracheids in the chart?
teacher_understanding.answer: Xylem, a complex permanent tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How do tracheids differ from vessel elements?
teacher_understanding.answer: Tracheids are elongated conducting cells without the perforation plates characteristic of vessel elements; water passes between tracheids through pits.

teacher_understanding.question: How are tracheids suited to water transport?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their dead, hollow interiors permit water movement, while lignified walls provide support and help resist collapse under tension.

items.exam_note: Identify tracheids as xylem conducting elements.

items.where_on_page: chart, Xylem box, second visible component
items.content: Vessels (Tracheae): listed component of Xylem.

teacher_understanding.question: Which tissue contains Vessels (Tracheae)?
teacher_understanding.answer: Xylem.

teacher_understanding.question: How do vessels differ from individual tracheids?
teacher_understanding.answer: Vessels consist of vessel elements joined end to end through perforated end walls, forming extended conducting channels; tracheids conduct between cells through pits.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this arrangement assist water flow?
teacher_understanding.answer: The connected lumens and perforated end walls provide a relatively open route along the vessel.

items.exam_note: Retain the alternative name Tracheae and distinguish plant vessels from other uses of 'trachea'.

items.where_on_page: chart, Xylem box, lowest fully visible component
items.content: Xylem parenchyma: listed component of Xylem.

teacher_understanding.question: Which complex tissue includes Xylem parenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: Xylem.

teacher_understanding.question: How does xylem parenchyma differ from mature tracheids and vessel elements?
teacher_understanding.answer: Xylem parenchyma cells are living, whereas mature tracheids and vessel elements are dead conducting cells.

teacher_understanding.question: How does living parenchyma contribute to xylem?
teacher_understanding.answer: It stores materials and assists lateral movement and exchange of substances within the tissue.

items.exam_note: Important living component of xylem.

items.content: Phloem: child of Complex under Permanent Tissue. Visible listed components: Sieve tubes; Companion cells; Phloem parenchyma. Lower box edge is cropped.

teacher_understanding.question: Which visible components are listed under Phloem?
teacher_understanding.answer: Sieve tubes, Companion cells and Phloem parenchyma.

teacher_understanding.question: How does phloem transport differ from xylem transport?
teacher_understanding.answer: Phloem mainly carries organic assimilates from sources to sinks, whereas xylem mainly carries water and mineral nutrients.

teacher_understanding.question: How do different phloem cell types cooperate?
teacher_understanding.answer: Sieve-tube elements provide conducting pathways, companion cells support their metabolism and transport processes, and parenchyma contributes storage and exchange.

items.exam_note: High-yield complex tissue and its visible components; lower list is cropped.

items.where_on_page: chart, Phloem box, first visible component
items.content: Sieve tubes: listed component of Phloem.

teacher_understanding.question: Which complex tissue contains Sieve tubes?
teacher_understanding.answer: Phloem.

teacher_understanding.question: How do sieve-tube elements differ from xylem vessel elements?
teacher_understanding.answer: Mature sieve-tube elements are living conducting cells that lack a nucleus in angiosperms; mature xylem vessel elements are dead and have lignified walls.

teacher_understanding.question: How do sieve tubes form a transport route?
teacher_understanding.answer: Sieve-tube elements join end to end, with sieve-plate pores allowing phloem sap to pass between them.

items.exam_note: Identify the conducting component of angiosperm phloem.

items.where_on_page: chart, Phloem box, second visible component
items.content: Companion cells: listed component of Phloem.

teacher_understanding.question: Which tissue includes Companion cells?
teacher_understanding.answer: Phloem.

teacher_understanding.question: How do companion cells differ from mature sieve-tube elements?
teacher_understanding.answer: Companion cells retain nuclei and dense metabolically active contents; mature sieve-tube elements lose their nuclei and are specialised for conduction.

teacher_understanding.question: Why are companion cells closely associated with sieve-tube elements?
teacher_understanding.answer: They provide metabolic support and participate in loading, unloading and maintaining the conducting system through close cellular connections.

items.exam_note: Common matching pair: sieve tubes and companion cells.

items.where_on_page: chart, Phloem box, lowest fully visible component
items.content: Phloem parenchyma: listed component of Phloem.

teacher_understanding.question: Which complex tissue contains Phloem parenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: Phloem.

teacher_understanding.question: How does phloem parenchyma differ in role from sieve tubes?
teacher_understanding.answer: Phloem parenchyma mainly contributes storage and local exchange, while sieve tubes specialise in long-distance transport of phloem sap.

teacher_understanding.question: How does parenchyma support the functioning of phloem?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its living cells store substances and help move materials laterally between conducting tissue and surrounding cells.

items.exam_note: Distinguish phloem parenchyma from xylem parenchyma by tissue membership.

wrong.problem: The image actually prints the typo 'Pholem parenchyma' in the bottom-right box of the classification chart, whereas items i30, i48, and i51 transcribe it as 'Phloem parenchyma' (unlike 'Paranchyma', whose printed typo was explicitly preserved).
wrong.fix: Optionally note the printed spelling 'Pholem parenchyma' while teaching the correct spelling 'Phloem parenchyma'.

checklist.note: Every statement is accurately traced to the book or clearly marked as outside knowledge, including careful corrections of printed inaccuracies (such as row 9 of the mitosis-meiosis table).
Explanations are thorough, biologically sound, and well-suited for UPSC/State PCS aspirants.
Maker notes clearly summarize the unit, explain key decisions with reasons, and flag uncertainties and cropped areas on the page.
Nothing is cut short, merged away, or left as 'etc.'; the cropped bottom of the image is explicitly documented.
Both image-only comparison tables, the organisation sequence, and the entire plant tissue classification chart are captured as items.
Only the running header (p0001-b0001) and page number (p0001-b0009) are marked as boilerplate.
All 11 rows of the Mitosis vs Meiosis table and all 4 rows of Table 7.3 appear as individual table_row items with column headers.
Every label, arrow, and branch in both the biological organisation sequence and the plant tissue classification tree is captured as its own item.
Arrow symbols and ploidy notations (where introduced in explanations) are read and explained accurately.
Questions and answers explain the underlying biological mechanisms (why and how) rather than merely restating the text.
Basis labels ('book' vs 'outside') are accurately assigned, and all outside knowledge is standard textbook biology.
Content types (definition, classification, cause_effect, structure, comparison) match the nature of each item and include all required questions.
Prerequisites are concrete, relevant biological concepts.
Exam importance ratings and notes are sensible for UPSC/State PCS.
The private-use glyph in native text block p0001-b0008 versus the rightward arrows in the image is properly reported in text_image_disagreements.
